```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(msprimeR.output = "msprime_ts")
```

msprimeR is an independent native R mirror of the
[msprime](https://tskit.dev/msprime/) simulator. It calls the original msprime
C library directly, so it needs no Python installation and produces the same
simulation tables as upstream msprime for the same parameters and random seed.
It is not an official upstream msprime release. Please cite the canonical
msprime paper by Baumdicker et al. (2022), *Efficient ancestry and mutation
simulation with msprime 1.0*, Genetics 220(3), iyab229,
<https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyab229>; `citation("msprimeR")` gives the
full reference.

```{r}
library(msprimeR)
```

## Simulating ancestry

`sim_ancestry()` simulates the genealogical history of a sample. Here we
sample 10 diploid individuals from a population of 10,000 individuals:

```{r}
ts <- sim_ancestry(samples = 10, population_size = 1e4, sequence_length = 1e5,
                   recombination_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 1)
ts
```

Mutations are added with `sim_mutations()`:

```{r}
mts <- sim_mutations(ts, rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 2)
mts$num_sites
head(ts_table(mts, "sites"))
```

## Tree sequence objects and tskitR

Results are tree sequences. When the
[tskitR](https://tskit.dev) package is installed, simulation functions return
`tskitR::TreeSequence` objects by default, which give access to the full tskit
toolkit (trees, statistics, genotypes, ...). This vignette sets
`options(msprimeR.output = "msprime_ts")`, so lightweight `msprime_ts` objects
are returned instead. These can be converted with `as_tskit()`, and written to
(or read from) the standard `.trees` format used by tskitR, tsdateR and tsinferR:

```{r}
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".trees")
ts_dump(mts, f)
ts_load(f)$num_mutations
```

The tables follow the tskit data model, with zero-based IDs:

```{r}
head(ts_table(ts, "nodes"))
```

## Demography

Demographic models are described with `Demography` objects. Populations are
referred to by name or by zero-based ID.

```{r}
demography <- Demography$new()
demography$add_population(name = "A", initial_size = 1e4)
demography$add_population(name = "B", initial_size = 5e3)
demography$add_population(name = "C", initial_size = 1e3)
demography$set_symmetric_migration_rate(c("A", "B"), 1e-4)
demography$add_population_split(time = 1000, derived = c("A", "B"), ancestral = "C")
demography
```

The `DemographyDebugger` describes the epochs of the model and computes
quantities such as coalescence rates:

```{r}
debug <- demography$debug()
debug$epoch_start_time
debug$mean_coalescence_time(c(A = 2))
```

Samples are taken from named populations:

```{r}
ts <- sim_ancestry(samples = c(A = 2, B = 3), demography = demography,
                   sequence_length = 1e4, recombination_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 3)
table(ts_table(ts, "nodes")$population[ts_table(ts, "nodes")$flags == 1])
```

Models can also be created from species trees (`Demography$from_species_tree()`)
and from [demes](https://popsim-consortium.github.io/demes-spec-docs/) YAML
models (`Demography$from_demes()`), and exported with `demography$to_demes()`.

## Ancestry and mutation models

Several ancestry models are available, and can be combined in sequence:

```{r}
ts <- sim_ancestry(5, population_size = 100, sequence_length = 1e4,
                   recombination_rate = 1e-6,
                   model = list(DiscreteTimeWrightFisher(duration = 20),
                                StandardCoalescent()),
                   random_seed = 4)
ts$num_trees
```

and many mutation models:

```{r}
mts <- sim_mutations(ts, rate = 1e-5, model = HKY(kappa = 2), random_seed = 5)
table(ts_table(mts, "sites")$ancestral_state)
```

## Reproducibility

Every simulation function takes a `random_seed`. If it is not given, a seed is
drawn from R's random number generator, so `set.seed()` makes analyses
reproducible.
